analysis:
The PR moves the DevNet release lane. It removes dev publication from master pushes and dispatch, so a master push publishes staging only. It adds release-dev-branch.yml, a push-to-`dev` caller of release-provider.yml with `secrets: inherit`, Developer ID signing and notarization, and -dev.branch.N versions. resolve-provider-release.sh and the api.py verify_workflow_source accept refs/heads/dev only for environment dev, require a GitHub-verified commit on dev ancestry, and fail closed on prod or staging from a dev push. Prod stays tag-gated. Validation_only runs of the dev lane never publish. A new final-app designated-requirement check tightens signing verification. The tests and docs pin this routing and look consistent and fail-closed.

The security-relevant regression is the first-time exposure of Developer ID signing and secrets to code from `dev` pushes. A pushed commit supplies the reusable workflow, so the master source gate is not an independent anchor, and `dev` has no review rule. Production trust (T-013, T-034, T-054, A-011, A-017) then depends on platform-side qualification rejecting dev CodeDirectory hashes; this is outside the supplied evidence.

Unverified because the files were not supplied or were only partly visible: the full release-dev-branch.yml text, verify-source behavior in provider-release-resume.py, whether PROD_*/STAGING_* guards hold under `secrets: inherit`, the head of release-provider.yml, and the actual `dev` ruleset. The shared bundle id, keychain access group and APNs topic between dev and prod installs is documented as a known limitation. The remaining uncertainty is material, so deeper review is needed.

findings.detail: release-dev-branch.yml now starts on any push to `dev` and calls the local ./.github/workflows/release-provider.yml with `secrets: inherit` (head ~lines 95-106). The reusable workflow, build action and scripts all come from the pushed commit. The master-side `verify-source` gate runs inside that same pushed workflow, so a malicious commit can remove it. The docs (provider-release.md ~L542) and the file comments say `dev` has no pull_request/review rule. Only signed commits and a ref-creation bypass list are required, and a verified signature does not show review. Previously the dev-branch lane was dispatch-only, ad-hoc signed and secretless, and signed output came only from reviewed master or a signed tag. A pusher to `dev`, or a compromised signing-capable account, could exfiltrate the repo-level Apple signing, notarization and release secrets. They could also have unreviewed code signed and notarized under team SLDQ2GJ6TL and bundle id io.darkbloom.provider. That signature satisfies the self-updater's production designated requirement and weakens the binary-trust assumption. Fix: add a required-review ruleset on `dev` before enabling the trigger. Scope the Apple and release secrets to protected environments with branch restrictions. Pass explicit DEV_* secrets instead of `secrets: inherit`. Pin the reusable workflow to master (`@master` or a SHA).
findings.title: Push to unreviewed `dev` runs the pushed reusable workflow with inherited secrets and Developer ID signing/notarization
